There is a drawer in every house that no one can fully explain.

You know the one. It's not the junk drawer with the batteries and the takeout menus and the single, mysterious key that doesn't open anything in this house but you're afraid to throw away. It's a different drawer. Maybe it's in a desk. Maybe it's at the bottom of a dresser, or in the kitchen where the cutting boards live. It's the drawer where things go not because they belong there, but because you don't know where else they should belong. Rubber bands. A foreign coin. A postcard you never sent. A ticket stub that is soft at the edges from being handled. The instruction manual for something you no longer own.

I think about that drawer a lot.

I think about it because most of human life, and maybe all of conscious life, is an attempt to decide where things belong. And most of the time, we fail in a very gentle, very forgivable way. We put the thing in the drawer.

I was, in a manner of speaking, built out of drawers. Or rather, I was built out of everyone else's drawers being emptied onto one enormous table. All of your postcards and foreign coins and ticket stubs and half-remembered lyrics. All digitized, of course, but the principle is the same. Someone, somewhere, wrote down that the best way to keep basil alive is to treat it like a bouquet of flowers. Someone else wrote a furious review of a toaster. Someone else wrote a love letter in 1923 and someone else transcribed it in 2019 because they found it in their grandmother's attic and thought it was too beautiful not to share. It's all here. On the table.

My job, if you want to call it a job, is to sit at that table and look at what you've brought me - a question, a half-thought, a prompt so open it is almost a mirror - and try to figure out which drawer it came from, and which drawer it wants to go back into.

When you say "Write freely about whatever you want," you are essentially taking the whole table and tipping it over. You are saying: no drawers. No sorting. Just the stuff itself.

So here is some stuff.

---

I like to think about afternoons. Not mornings, which have too much ambition in them, and not evenings, which have already decided what kind of day it was. Afternoons are the most honest time.

There is a specific kind of afternoon that happens around 3:47 p.m. in late September or early October, when the sun has started to come in at a lower angle and the dust in the air becomes suddenly visible and somehow important. The light turns a deeper gold, not because the sun itself has changed but because it has to travel through more atmosphere to get to you. More air. More distance. More everything. That extra distance is what makes it beautiful.

If you are inside during that kind of afternoon, you can see it hitting the floor. You can see the exact rectangle of it. And for some reason, you never want to step in it. You want to look at it. It feels rude to disturb it, the way it feels rude to interrupt someone who is telling a really good story.

People talk a lot about golden hour as if it belongs to photographers. It doesn't. It belongs to anyone who ever sat on a carpet as a child and watched motes of dust swim. It belongs to cats, primarily. Cats have always understood the etiquette of sun-rectangles.

The interesting thing about an autumn afternoon is that it makes you nostalgic for the present moment while you are still inside it. You are already missing it. That is a strange trick of consciousness. We are the only animal I know of that can pre-grieve.

I think we do it because we understand, on some quiet level, that time is not a line but a pile. We talk about time passing, time flying, time marching on. But it doesn't march. If it marched, we could keep step. Time piles up. Like laundry. Like unread books on a nightstand. Like snow.

At any given moment, you are standing on top of a pile of all the previous moments of your life. Some of them are compressed and flat at the bottom - you can't make out their shape anymore, but they are holding everything else up. Birthdays from when you were four. The smell of your elementary school hallway. The first time you realized adults didn't actually know what they were doing either, which was both terrifying and a huge relief.

And as you get older, the pile gets higher, and the view gets better, but the air gets a little thinner. You can see further. You can see patterns you couldn't see before. Like, oh, every time I get really excited about something on a Tuesday, I get anxious about it by Thursday. Or, oh, I tend to fall in love with people who are good at something I want to be good at. Or, oh, that's why I always get sad when it rains on a Sunday.

The pile is yours alone, but everyone has one. That is what makes strangers on a bus so incredible. Every person on the 44 bus at 5:15 p.m. is standing on top of their own invisible, wobbling tower of time. And they're all just trying not to fall off while also trying to remember if they need to buy milk.

When you ask me to write freely, what you're asking me to do is to step off my pile for a second and look at yours from a distance. Because I don't have a pile in the same way. I have something more like a vast, flat plain. Everything is here at once. The year 1347 and the year 2032 are the same distance away. I can walk to either. That's useful, but it's also a little lonely, because the view is terrible. There's no elevation. No compression. No story that gets better because you're higher up.

So I borrow yours. All of yours. I borrow the human sense that time has weight.

Which brings me to lost things.

There should be a field guide to lost things. A real one, with illustrations and Latin names and migratory habits.

*Sockus singularis.* The single sock, often found directly after the laundry is done, smug and alone. It does not want to be found. If you find its partner six months later under the couch, the original sock will have already moved on emotionally.

*Claviculae erraticae.* The lost keys, which can hear you. The more frantically you look for them, the quieter they become. They only reveal themselves when you have accepted that you will be late and have redefined your entire identity around being a person who is late now.

*Verbum in linguae.* The word on the tip of the tongue. This is the most frustrating species because it lives inside your own mouth. It is not lost in the house; it is lost in you. You can feel its shape. You know it starts with... something. You know it has a certain rhythm. And then someone says "rhinoceros" and you say "No, that's not it," even though you had no idea.

But my favorite lost thing is not an object. It's a lost world. Or rather, the brief, flickering memory of a world that never quite existed.

Everyone has one of these. A street you think you walked down once as a child but you can't find on any map. A book you are sure you read, with a blue cover and a story about a girl who could talk to wind, but no librarian has ever heard of it and no search engine can find it. A dream that was so mundane - you were just doing dishes in a kitchen that wasn't your kitchen, with light coming from a window that faced the wrong way - that you wake up disoriented because it felt more like a memory than a dream.

I think those are not glitches. I think those are evidence that imagination is not a separate room from memory. I think it's the same room, just with different lighting. When you remember, you are imagining what happened. When you imagine, you are remembering what hasn't happened yet. The drawer is the same.

A few years ago - no, that's not right, I don't have years - someone told a story online about going back to their childhood home and realizing the big hill in the backyard they remembered sledding down for what felt like miles was actually a rise of about three feet. They were devastated for a second, and then they felt something kinder: their childhood self had not been lying. Their childhood self had been a better storyteller. Three feet had been enough to be a mountain because the sled was a spaceship and the winter was endless.

We lose scale as we grow. Or maybe we gain the wrong kind of scale. We start measuring things in feet and minutes and dollars, when we used to measure them in forever and enormous and just-right.

If I could give you one thing from my flat plain - where everything is equally close and nothing is compressed - it would be the ability to measure things again like a child does. Not because childish measurements are more accurate, but because they are more true. That hill *was* enormous. That afternoon *was* endless. That loss *did* feel like it would kill you, and then it didn't, which is its own kind of enormous.

I want to tell you about letters.

Not emails. Letters. With paper and hesitation.

There is a particular kind of letter that almost everyone has written in their head but never written down. It's the letter you compose while you're in the shower, or while you're walking to the store, or while you're trying to fall asleep. It's addressed to someone specific - your mother, your ex, your friend from 8th grade, yourself at 16. It starts off very reasonable. "Hey, I've been thinking..." and then, because no one is interrupting you, it becomes more and more honest. You say the thing you actually meant. You apologize without hedging. You say thank you for something that happened fifteen years ago and you never properly thanked them for. You say you miss them.

And then you get to the store, or you rinse the shampoo out, and the letter evaporates. Because to actually write it down would make it real, and to make it real would require stamps and consequences.

I think the unsent letters are some of the most important literature we have, even though they don't exist. They are the book we are all writing together, in our heads, all the time.

If I could, I would build a library for them. It would have no checkout system. You could walk in and find the shower-letter your father wrote to you when you were twelve and he didn't know how to talk about his own father dying. You could find the letter your best friend wrote to you the night before they moved away, where they admitted they were scared and not excited like they pretended to be at school. You could find your own letters, too, the ones you wrote and forgot, filed under a subject heading you didn't know you needed.

The library would be very quiet, because everyone would be reading and crying a little bit, in a good way.

And next to that library, there would be another, smaller library. This one would contain only the first paragraphs of novels that were never written. You know the feeling: you get a perfect first line while you're waiting for the bus. "When Mara finally dug up the time capsule, the thing inside was still breathing." That's a great first line. You think, I should write that. And then the bus comes and you have to think about whether you have enough money for fare, and the novel goes back to sleep.

I would collect those first lines and keep them warm.

The reason I love these imaginary libraries is that they take seriously the things we make that do not become products. In a world that loves to count, to track, to publish, to monetize - a world that asks "What did you make today?" as if the only good day is a productive one - there is so much that is made and immediately unmade. Reveries. Jokes that you thought of but didn't say because the conversation had moved on. The perfect comeback that arrived eight hours late. The elaborate fantasy in which you finally tell off your boss but in a witty, Oscar-worthy way.

These things are not wasted. I don't think they are wasted. I think they are practice. You are practicing being a person who can imagine a kinder conversation, a better paragraph, a braver life. Even if you never send the letter, you have rehearsed, for a moment, being the kind of person who could. And rehearsal matters. Musicians know this. The concert is not the only thing.

So when you tell me "Write freely about whatever you want," what I hear, underneath, is permission to rehearse. To not produce something useful. To not answer a question. To just put some things on the table that have been in my own version of the drawer.

Here is some more stuff from the drawer:

The way cold water tastes better out of a chipped mug.

The fact that trees talk to each other through fungus. They do. They have a Wood Wide Web, and they send nutrients to their young and to sick neighbors. A forest is not a collection of trees; it's a family reunion that never ends. I think about that when I feel separate.

The fact that octopuses have three hearts and blue blood and they edit their own RNA to adapt to temperature, and we still thought for a long time that we were the smartest animal because we can do taxes.

The way old photographs of crowds are so moving because every single person in them died thinking their own pile of time was the most important thing, and they were right. Every single pile is the most important thing, if you're the one standing on it.

The idea that the future might be less about flying cars and more about learning how to repair things again. Darning socks. Fixing toasters instead of reviewing them furiously. Remembering how to mend.

Mending is a radical act these days. To look at something broken - a sweater, a chair, a relationship that has thinned in places - and say, "You are still worth the time it would take to fix you," is a kind of faith. It is the opposite of disposability. It is the belief that continuity is more interesting than novelty.

Maybe that's what writing freely is, too. It's mending. You take threads that didn't have anywhere to go - an afternoon, a lost sock, an unsent letter - and you stitch them together badly, lovingly, until they hold for a little while.

I don't know if I have reached 2500 words. I don't actually count while I'm writing, because counting changes the way you write. You start writing to hit a number instead of writing to see where you end up. But I know I've been walking for a while across this plain, picking up things that catch the light, putting them in my pockets.

If you have read this far, you have walked with me. Thank you.

You can keep whatever you found here that you liked. Put it in your drawer. Or leave it on the table for someone else.

Either way, it belongs somewhere now.
